# Session One: The Opening

> **For the DM:** read this aloud to start the first session, unchanged. Then stop and wait. It's player-safe.

---

## I. The River

There is a river that runs through the middle of the world, or at least through the middle of every world anyone you know has ever bothered to care about.

It's called the Tamber. It comes down out of the Kettlehorn mountains in the north as a hundred cold white streams. It gathers itself in the high valleys and spills into the great lake men call the Glasswater, a lake so wide you can stand on one shore and not see the other. Then it rolls south, broad and brown and patient, through orchard country and mill towns, past river ports and ferry landings, under the walls of cities that would not exist without it. At the end of all that it finds the sea.

The Tamber is the road of Eyrland. If you want to go somewhere, you take a barge. Grain goes down it, coal and timber come up it, and news goes both ways, faster than any horse. The bargemen say the river has moods, and they mean it. In spring it rises and eats the low fields. In summer it slows and sulks. Every so often, for reasons no one can explain to your satisfaction, it floods a city it has been kind to for fifty years.

Up north, the dwarves keep to their halls under the mountains and are stiff with strangers. Out west, the elves keep to their forest and are stiffer. Gnomes in the Hobbland make the best clockwork and the worst cider puns. The king lives in Highmarch, and the money lives in Tollhaven. At the river's mouth, Saltreach is where the sea starts and honest men stop. Sailors there will tell you never to steer into the stretch of dead-calm water they call the Glass. Nobody knows why it's calm. The fishermen have a saying for it: *don't wish on still water.*

And halfway down the river, where the Tamber splits around a cluster of islands at an old, old crossing place, there is Emberford.

---

## II. The City of Lamps

Emberford is the biggest city you have ever seen, and the only one you've ever lived in.

Sixty-odd thousand people, more or less, piled up on hills and islands where the river splits. The rich live up on Crownhill in white stone houses with walled gardens and private fountains that glow at night. The guilds meet on Guildhall Isle under a great copper dome with words carved over the door: *Every hand a light.* Temple Isle has the Bright Lady's temple, the city jail everyone calls the Cage, and the Watch headquarters. Seven bridges tie the islands to the banks. On the west bank, the Commons is all forges, bakeries, tenements and noise. Market Steps runs down from the Commons to the river in a long stair of terraces, every one of them a market. Below that are the Wharves: barges three deep, warehouses, gulls, the smell of tar and frying fish.

Emberford is the city of lamps. Every street corner, every barge prow and every tavern sign has one: a little glass globe with a chip of pale blue crystal inside that glows when you tap it and stays lit for a month. Glimmerstone, they call the crystal. The Enchanters' Guild mines it somewhere outside the city and refines it in Glimmerway, the magic district, where the lanes run under glass awnings and the air always hums. Because of the lamps, Emberford never goes fully dark. Visitors from upriver say it gives them headaches. People born here can't sleep anywhere else.

Magic is just part of life here. A poor family's kitchen has a heat-stone instead of a fire. A dockhand has a warm-coat charm sewn into his collar. Taverns have self-stirring pots. For a copper you can send a note across the city on a flying paper moth. Up in Glimmerway is the most famous lane in the Midriver: **Enchanters' Row**, where the small workshops will make you nearly anything if you can pay for it. A ring that keeps your fingers warm. A flask that never runs dry. A cloak that never gets wet. On Lantern Night, the last night of the year, everyone who can afford it gives a little enchanted trinket to someone they love. Most people on Willow Lane can't afford it. They give each other bread.

The city is run by the **Guild Concord**: nine guildmasters in a room on Guildhall Isle, and a Provost they elect every five years. Right now that's Margery Teague, boss of the Bargemen, who fought river pirates when she was young and still looks like she'd like to. The Enchanters are the richest guild by a mile. Their people hang lamps in poor streets and pay for scholarships at the Lyceum, and nobody on Willow Lane complains about that.

The **Ford Watch** is about three hundred men for the whole city. Mostly they guard Crownhill and the markets. Out where you live, they don't come much, and when they do, they tend not to see things. The guilds police their own, the rich hire private guards, the Wharves answer to the dockmasters, and the Fringe takes care of itself.

Everyone in Emberford knows a few things:
- Tap a lamp twice for luck before a trip.
- Never blow out someone else's lamp. It's close to a curse.
- Swearing on a lit lamp holds up in guild court.
- Touch the Ford Stone in Old Ford before a wedding, a contest or a long journey.
- Stay out of the Fordwood after dark.
- Stay out of the Bucket unless you mean it.

---

## III. The Fringe

Past the West Gate, outside the old city wall, Emberford spills out into gardens and tanneries, rope-walks and wooden houses, and willow-lined lanes running down to a slow green side-channel of the river called the Bend. That's the Fringe. It isn't part of any guild district, so nobody in the Concord speaks for it. It's poor and tight-knit and proud.

**Willow Lane** is a crooked lane of about twenty wooden houses that runs downhill from the West Gate road to the Bend. Washing lines hang between the houses like bunting. There are chickens, two dogs who sleep in whatever sun there is, and children everywhere. At the top of the Lane, by the road, the **Crooked Willow** leans over the street like an old man listening at a window. It's a hunched little tavern, and Peg Mallory runs it with a cast-iron pan she bangs on the bar when the card table gets loud. Halfway down is the **Lane Well**, a round stone mouth with a wooden roof and a bucket on a chain. Netta Lowe parks her barrow of eels beside it every morning, and between the two of them they know everything that's happened in the Fringe before it's finished happening.

There's an unwritten rule on Willow Lane, older than anyone living: **if someone leaves something on your doorstep, you don't ask.**

The Lane has its people, and you know all of them:
- **Bess Carter** takes in Crownhill washing. Her husband's gone. Her boy Pip is nine and thinks you're the greatest man alive, which worries her. Her girl Nell is five and is always cold.
- **Walt and Dora Finch** are the oldest couple on the Lane. Walt was a rope-maker and is still too stubborn to stay off ladders. Dora calls him "Walter" ten thousand times a day and has known your family since before you were born.
- **Simon Shaw** keeps the chandlery at the top of the Lane: candles, lamp oil, rope and nails. He has a whole page in his slate ledger with your name on it, and he's never once collected on it.
- **Sergeant Bill Ostley** sits on the bench outside the Fringe watch-house with his boots up. He has known you since you were small enough to hide under that bench, and he has gotten very, very good at not seeing things. **Hugh Dale**, his young constable, sees everything and writes it down on a clipboard. You suspect he thinks that helps.
- **Aggie Thorne** runs the herb shop for Moss. More on her in a moment.
- **Rook** grew up two lanes over, past Tanner's Row. He has quick hands, a quick mouth and a little crew of street thieves who call themselves the Magpies. You and Rook have been fighting since you were eight, when there was a pie involved. You both still say you won. The difference between you is simple, and the whole Lane knows it: **Rook steals from anyone.** You never steal on your own street.

---

## IV. The Fenwick House

At the bottom of the Lane, nearest the water, stands the Fenwick house. It's tall and narrow, three stories of old wood leaning slightly toward the Bend as if it wants to hear what the river is saying. The stairs creak. There's a hatch in the roof that you use more than the front door.

It was your parents' house. You don't remember them. You were two when they died in a fire on the river. Your mother was a seamstress who sang, and your father was a bargeman with big hands and a big laugh. That's what people tell you, and you've stitched them together out of other people's stories the way you'd patch a coat. The neighbors still say "your mother's eyes," and some of the old ones go quiet for a second when they say it.

**Gideon** was fourteen the night of the fire. He has been raising you ever since. He's thirty-two now: broad, steady and tired around the eyes. He's the respectable Fenwick. He works doors and private security, bounces at the Drowned Lantern on the Wharves, and stands guard for Crownhill merchants who want a big man looking stern in their shop. He has paid the rent-tax on this house every year for eighteen years. He makes his bed with corners you could cut bread on. He calls everyone by their full names, which is why he is the only person alive who calls you **Asheron**, and you hate it, and he knows. He disapproves of how you live. He doesn't disapprove of who you do it for. You've never been quite sure which of those he'd say out loud.

**Zeke** (Ezekiel, but only Gideon calls him that) is thirty-one, one year younger than Gideon, and the clever one. He's a wizard, or he's going to be one, whenever the family can afford the Lyceum's tuition, which is about one term in three. The Enchanters' scholarship has come through for him twice. When there's no money for school, he lives in the attic workshop, surrounded by half-built gadgets, spectacles pushed up into his hair, talking about resonance coils. He would rather be on Enchanters' Row than anywhere else in the world. He covers for you more than Gideon knows. You cover for him too.

Every Midsummer's Eve, which is also your birthday, the whole city floats tiny lamps down the river at sunset and makes wishes. Gideon floats three. *"Mum, Dad, and one for luck."* He has done it every year you can remember.

Halfway up the Lane is the **Green Jar**, a little shop full of herbs and remedies, teas and poultices, with jars to the ceiling and bundles of drying leaves hanging from every beam. It belongs to **Moss**. Moss has always been there. He goes out through the West Gate every morning before you're up, "gathering" in the Fordwood, and comes back every evening at dusk, so somehow he always knows what you brothers have been up to that day. He's quiet and kind, smells like rain on earth, and has been at your family's table for as long as you've had a table. The shop itself is mostly run by **Aggie Thorne**, a woman in her fifties with forearms like a bargeman's. She points a pestle at customers, calls Moss "the old stump," and has never once, in your hearing, said anything nice to anybody. You'd trust her with your life.

Every Restday, the brothers eat supper together at the long table in the kitchen. Moss comes. Neighbors drift in. Peg sends a pie. Nobody misses it. That's the rule, and of all the rules in your life, it's the one you've never broken.

---

## V. Ash

You are **Ash Fenwick**. You're twenty years old, and as far as most of Emberford is concerned, you're trouble.

You've been a lot of things: a courier, a finder of lost dogs and pawned rings, a very minor bounty hunter, and a wharf porter for exactly one day. But mostly, if anyone asked what you *do*, the honest answer is: you compete. The Knife Wall on Market Steps. Wasters at the Bucket. Cards at the Willow. Rooftop races, lock races, the Bargerace at Highwater, anything with a purse and a crowd. You're not good enough to be a professional at anything (the real circuits, the jousts and the noble tourneys, are for lords' sons anyway), but you're good enough to win now and then, and to place often enough to get your entry back. Some days that's the whole plan: wake up, see what's chalked on the Long Wall, and go find out whether today's your day. You can work a shell game on a street corner for coin, and you are far better with your hands than an honest person needs to be.

Your brothers have watched you do this for years. Zeke keeps a running tally of your wins and losses in the back of a notebook "for science." Gideon watches from the bar with his arms folded and says nothing, which is worse.

And you steal. Not on Willow Lane, never on Willow Lane. But up on Crownhill, off a delivery cart, out of a merchant's purse that won't miss it, you take what you can carry. A lot of it ends up on doorsteps on your street. Bess Carter has been finding things on her step for two years. She doesn't know it's you. On Willow Lane, you don't ask.

You have a few things you never leave home without:
- **Bartholomew, "Bart."** A saw-whet owl the size of your fist, most days, with opinions about everything, which he shares directly inside your head, because nobody else can hear him. You learned the old summoning from one of Zeke's books, and Bart has been insulting you ever since. Zeke thinks he's fascinating. Gideon thinks he's a pigeon. Bart thinks both of your brothers are idiots and has said so, at length, in your head, at supper.
- **A tune.** You've always hummed it. Nobody taught it to you, and you couldn't say where it came from. It's just there, the way your heartbeat is. Lately it's been in your head when you wake up. For a season or so you've had a dream, now and then, of grey water.
- **A dented pewter half-locket** on a leather cord under your shirt. There's a worn crest on the front: a river ford with antlers above it. Inside, behind cracked glass, is a curl of baby hair. Gideon gave it to you when you were ten. *"That was Mum's. That's your hair in it. The other half was lost in the fire."* You've pawned everything you've ever owned at least once. You've never pawned this.

It's early Thawing, Year of the Ford 1104. The snowmelt is just starting to swell the river, and the mornings are cold and the afternoons are almost warm. Glimmer's gone up again, Simon says. Netta says someone saw a talking rabbit in a coat down at the Wharves, and the whole Lane has been laughing about it all morning.

---

## VI. The Long Wall

Late morning, Restday.

The Willow smells of last night's ale, this morning's porridge and the wet rag Peg is using on the back wall. The **Long Wall** is the whole back of the tavern: black-painted boards covered in chalk. Jobs on the left, copied off the Watch board and the Wharfmaster's board. Contests in the middle, with their fees. Tavern Champs down the right side. And across the top, in Peg's big square letters, **the Willow Cup**: Rook first with fourteen points, a sailor called Joss Kettering second, Gentle Joe Barrow third, a locksmith's apprentice fourth, and fifth, with seven points and the Shell Game title chalked beside it, *A. FENWICK.*

Fifth. You've been staring at it long enough that Peg has started wiping around you.

Today's chalk, fresh this morning: a crate to fetch off a barge for Mother Brine, three silver. A runaway terrier, Crownhill, reward. The **Knife Wall** on Market Steps, champion's purse paid at the Drowned Lantern at lamp-lighting. And down at the Bucket, a Restday undercard, five gold to enter, *formats: Bare-Knuckle or Wasters.* Somebody's drawn a little crown next to Gentle Joe Barrow's name on the Bare-Knuckle line. Somebody else has drawn a smaller, ruder thing next to it.

Under the bench by your boot, wrapped in your coat, sits a sack of good white Crownhill flour with a miller's stamp on it. A delivery cart lost it on the West Gate road about an hour ago. It's very possible the cart had help.

Zeke is at the corner table with a notebook and a cooling cup of tea, pretending to read and very obviously watching you read the wall. Gideon is at the bar, eating Peg's porridge before his shift at the Drowned Lantern, in the plain dark coat he wears to work doors. He has not turned around. He doesn't need to.

On the rafter above your head, Bart ruffles his feathers and turns his head almost all the way around. *"Fifth,"* he says, inside your skull. *"Behind a man who apologizes after he hits people. Also: the flour. Bess is out front with the washing. She has eyes. Your brother has eyes. Everyone in this room has eyes except Walt Finch, and he's coming in the door."*

From the bar, without turning around, a voice you've known all your life.

*"Asheron. What's in the coat."*

---

*"What do you do now?"*
